paras: The lynching of Bert Wilkinson took place in Silverton, Colorado, on the evening of Sunday, September 4, 1881, when a party of masked men overpowered the guards at the town jail and hanged him. Wilkinson was accused of killing Silverton's city marshal about ten days earlier, and his Black companion, Jim Catrin, had already been lynched from the same jail. Papers across the country noted the case for Wilkinson's composure on the gallows, his betrayal by the outlaw Ike Stockton, and his respectable Indiana family.

According to a Rico correspondent of the Chicago Tribune, Wilkinson and a man the paper called a "coon" named Jim Catrin took part in a saloon shooting north of Durango in which the saloonkeeper was killed. The two then appeared in Silverton with Dyson Eskridge, and City Marshal D. C. ("Clate") Ogsbury was shot while trying to arrest them, living only long enough to name Wilkinson as his killer. The first wire from Silverton, dated August 26, said the whole town was aroused and that "the murderers will be lynched if captured."

Catrin, described in a Denver dispatch as "a negro boy," was taken from the Silverton jail and hanged by the town's Vigilance Committee shortly after the marshal's death. Wilkinson was captured in the Needle Mountains by Ike Stockton, and a Denver report of August 31 noted "strong feeling in favor of lynching Wilkinson."

Wilkinson's sister, Mrs. Flora W. Pyle, told the Dolores News that Stockton, his friend, had separated him from Eskridge and taken him at gunpoint, saying "Money is what makes men in this country." After being held under guard at Animas City, Wilkinson was turned over on Saturday to the San Juan County sheriff and lodged in the Silverton jail, and his sister stayed in town until Sunday. The Rico correspondent believed her presence prevented a lynching on Saturday night, and she was told on Sunday that he would be hanged whether she stayed or not.

About 9:30 that Sunday evening, according to the Laramie Times, masked men overpowered the guards and the jailer, entered the jail, put a noose around Wilkinson's neck and asked if he had anything to say. He answered "Nothing, gentlemen. Adios," climbed onto a chair and helped the "vigilantes" hang him. The Rico account adds that he adjusted the noose himself, saying "Boys, I'll help you all I can," regretted that he could not shoot Stockton, asked not to be photographed, and kicked the chair away.

No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry into the lynching appears in the coverage. Stockton was shot by La Plata County officers in Durango later in September and died after his leg was amputated, and Eskridge was captured in New Mexico and was expected to be taken to Silverton. A letter from Durango dated September 28 and signed "Twenty-Two of Us" warned Silverton's mayor that vengeance would follow if Eskridge were lynched, and said the town had hanged "the Kid, who was innocent of any crime."

Only white papers covered the lynching, from Colorado and Nevada to Illinois, Virginia and North Carolina, between mid-September and mid-October. Wire briefs called Wilkinson "a well-known desperado" who had killed "no less than three men" and reported his death without comment. A Colorado state-news column bracketed him with his companion: "The 'Black Kid' and Burt Wilkinson, murderers of Marshal Ogsbury, of Silverton, are dead. Lynched."

The Chicago Tribune ran the fullest account under the headline "LYNCHED," calling the hanging the "closing scene of a most thrilling tragedy" and saying he "paid in full the debt" of his crime, while printing his sister's attack on Stockton's treachery. Late in September the Richmond Dispatch and the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic printed "A Blue-Blooded Outlaw," which traced his family to a former governor of Indiana, called the murder "wanton, brutal, and cowardly," and admired his "bravado" at death. The Durango Southwest, reprinting the threat letter, said it did not approve of lynching but that incompetent officials made "strangling a necessity at times."

The Laramie Times placed the hanging inside the jail, while the Rico correspondent wrote that the masked men "took Wilkinson out" without naming where he died. Wilkinson's guilt also rested on Silverton accounts and the marshal's dying words, and his sister said he neither denied nor admitted the killing.

bases: A party of masked men took Wilkinson from the Silverton jail and hanged him while he was held on a murder accusation (A15, A21).
Wilkinson was hanged by a 'party of masked men' called 'vigilantes' who overpowered the jail guards, without any trial, for the killing of the town marshal (A15, A21, A26).

The Laramie Times account (A15) and the Rico correspondence of the Chicago Tribune (A21) independently describe the Sunday-night jail lynching, and Colorado and national briefs confirm it (A22, A23, A29).
